demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: Kofi, a 55-year-old painter from Ghana, had always found solace in his craft. The vibrant colors and textures of his work provided a sense of peace and fulfillment, but ever since the unexpected death of his younger brother, Kwame, that peace had been shattered. The tragedy struck suddenly when Kwame collapsed during a family gathering, a heart attack that no one saw coming. The chaos that ensued-the sirens of the ambulance, the frantic calls for help-had imprinted on Kofi's mind, and now, every time he heard an ambulance in the distance or saw flashing lights, his heart raced and his body tensed, as if the event were happening all over again. Each of these triggers sent a jolt of fear through him, convincing him that danger was imminent, as if he were back in that moment of crisis, heightening his sense of threat with every reminder of his brother's death. Every time he heard an ambulance, the thought settled in his mind with unsettling clarity: this is what life had become - a constant reminder of loss and impending danger. Hearing an ambulance would instantly pull him back to that chaotic day, conjuring memories of frantic cries and desperate attempts to save his brother, which felt as vivid as if they were unfolding once more. The sound of an approaching siren would send his heart racing, leading him to feel that danger lurked around every corner, as if he were perpetually at risk of experiencing another devastating loss. These triggers not only heightened his sense of danger but also flooded him with memories that he couldn't fully grasp. He often felt as though he were trapped in a loop of grief, where emotional waves crashed over him without clear images-just a suffocating sense of loss. The aftermath of Kwame's death left Kofi feeling as though he no longer recognized himself. He was a man who had always been grounded, but now he felt adrift and isolated, as if the world had moved on while he remained trapped in a moment of devastation. He found it increasingly difficult to connect with others, believing they could never understand his pain. This belief that he was permanently changed and fundamentally vulnerable made every interaction feel risky, leaving him braced for the possibility of judgment or misunderstanding from others. His conviction that he was now a target in a world filled with hidden dangers caused him to feel threatened by even the simplest conversations, as if every interaction could expose him to further emotional harm. Once he had concluded that he was fundamentally vulnerable, even friendly exchanges felt like potential traps, leaving him on edge and hyper-aware of every word spoken. Conversations about loss, which he had once navigated with ease, became unbearable. When coworkers at the painting site shared their own stories of loss, Kofi felt a sharp pang in his chest and the familiar tension in his shoulders, as though their words were reigniting his own grief. Every mention of loss sent a jolt through him, reinforcing the belief that he was now fundamentally vulnerable and forever changed, making those painful memories surge to the forefront of his mind. This pain reinforced his belief that he would never be able to escape the shadow of his brother's death, making the memories of that day feel more acute and vivid, as if they were further evidence of his failure. Each mention of loss felt like a reminder that his life had been irrevocably altered, and he had become a mere shadow of his former self. At night, Kofi's vulnerability intensified. The darkness that once provided a comforting embrace now felt threatening. He lay awake, alert and on edge, listening to every creak of the house, every rustle outside. This hyper-vigilance made it difficult for him to rest, and the growing fear that something might happen to those he loved only compounded his anxiety. The relentless sense of danger he carried transformed ordinary noises into harbingers of catastrophe, making every creak of the house feel like a prelude to something terrible, and amplifying his memories of loss. Living in this constant state of alertness, Kofi found that even the slightest sounds would trigger vivid recollections of that fateful day, each reminding him that his world was still filled with hidden threats. He would often replay the day of Kwame's death in his mind, struggling to reconcile the vivid, haunting images with the deep emotional turmoil they evoked. After each memory surfaced, he couldn't shake the feeling that the threat of loss was still present - an ever-looming shadow that transformed his surroundings into a landscape of risk and fear. His conviction that he should have seen the signs of Kwame's heart attack made those memories sharper, as if each recollection served as proof of his failure to protect his brother, locking him in a cycle of guilt and pain. With each memory that surfaced, he couldn't shake the belief that he had missed crucial signals, reinforcing his sense of vulnerability and feeding his anxiety about future losses. The weight of his grief felt like a physical presence, heavy and inescapable, and he believed it had destroyed the life he once cherished. As he grappled with his grief, Kofi noticed a cycle forming. The triggers heightened his feelings of threat and danger, and in turn, the constant threat made the memories of that day feel even more potent. Whenever he saw an ambulance or heard someone mention loss, it triggered not only memories of Kwame's death but also the pervasive belief that he had lost a part of himself that could never be reclaimed. This destructive loop was exhausting; he felt like he was drowning in a sea of pain with no shore in sight. Kofi's sense of isolation deepened as he retreated further into himself. His belief that he was fundamentally different and exposed made even mundane encounters feel fraught with potential triggers, prompting him to withdraw from situations where he might be reminded of his grief. "These memories acted as triggers too, making ordinary moments feel charged with the potential for grief, as if the weight of his loss could surface at any moment." He began avoiding social gatherings, fearing the possibility of encountering conversations about loss, which only reinforced his belief that he was now different from everyone else. The fear of being unable to control his emotions in public made him seek refuge in his solitude, leaving him feeling even more disconnected from his friends and family. This pervasive belief that the world was now a dangerous place meant that even the most mundane situations felt charged with potential threat, causing him to withdraw from social interactions that might otherwise have been comforting. "The sound of the sirens carried with it an overwhelming sense of danger that felt as real as the day he lost Kwame, sending his body into a state of alarm that reaffirmed his belief that he was always under threat." Each day felt like a battle against a tide of memories and emotions that he could no longer manage, and the thought of seeking help remained a distant consideration, shrouded in shame and uncertainty. "Each time these memories surfaced, they would amplify his sense of threat, leaving him with the gut-wrenching belief that the danger of loss was still present, lurking just beyond his reach." The more intensely he relived these memories, the more assured he became that asking for help was a sign of weakness, reinforcing his belief that he was unworthy of support and further isolating him from others. "The persistent sense of threat he carried transformed the past into a living danger, as if each memory was a reminder that he had not only lost his brother but had also somehow invited that loss into his life." After months of grappling with the weight of his grief, Kofi finally reached a breaking point. "The continuous threat he felt from these memories made him question his ability to navigate the world, further isolating him and amplifying his anxiety about seeking support." During a particularly difficult night, he felt an overwhelming urge to reach out for help. "The belief that he was fundamentally changed by his loss loomed over him, making him wonder if he could ever truly escape the shadows of that day and the threat that came with it." The isolation had become unbearable, and he was terrified of what his life would look like if he continued down this path. Kofi hoped that by seeking support, he might begin to reclaim the pieces of himself that felt lost, though he was haunted by the fear that he might never fully heal from the trauma of losing Kwame. His belief that he was permanently altered by the loss kept pulling him back to that day, as if he needed to constantly relive the moment he felt he had failed. "Each trigger would pull memories to the forefront of his mind, flooding him with vivid recollections of that chaotic day, as if he were reliving it all over again." "Having decided he was fundamentally vulnerable, Kofi walked into conversations already anticipating danger, making him hyper-aware of every word spoken as if each one could expose him to further emotional harm." "His conviction that he was now a target made even the simplest discussions about loss feel like potential traps, heightening his anxiety and leading to memories of his brother's death flooding back." "The haunting memories of that day reinforced his negative appraisals, leading him to believe he had failed Kwame and that this failure defined who he was."
